This entry is from the baptism register of the Reformed Protestant Dutch Church of Albany, recorded on 18 March 1750 (Old Style, equivalent to 18 March 1750/51 in modern reckoning). His father is identified as Jacob Perry, a cordwainer (a shoemaker working in new leather) of Albany, and his mother as Elisabeth Witbeck of Albany — the Dutch Reformed church of the period customarily recorded a mother under her birth surname, so the family name is Perry but the record preserves her Witbeck maiden name. Two sponsors stood at the baptism: Hendrick Witbeck, who shares the mother's surname and may well be her brother or another Witbeck relation, and Maria Van Deusen.

The next step is to check whether Jacob Perry, Elisabeth Witbeck, or Hendrick Witbeck appear in other Albany Dutch Reformed records that could confirm family relationships and the Witbeck connection.

Good — tools are loaded. Calendar check first: Norway adopted the Gregorian calendar in 1700, so this 1817 Stavanger register is firmly Gregorian — no date conversion needed.

Now fetching the indexed record to get the full persona fields and locate the image ARK.

Good — the index record is in hand. Key observations before I go to the image:

- **Father given name**: indexed as "Tollev" — but the child's full name recorded elsewhere as *Kristian Fredrik **Tollefsen** Birkeland* means the father's given name was almost certainly **Tollef**, not Tollev. The patronymic suffix *-sen* derives directly from the father's name.
- **Father surname "Nadnesen"**: flagged as suspect — this is the key identity element I need to verify against the original register image.
- **Father's residence**: Birkeland — consistent with the child's farm byname.
- **Mother**: Inger Larsdatter.

"Nadnesen" is not a recognisable Norwegian patronymic root. A very common OCR/handwriting slip in Rogaland records is misreading **Aadne** → producing "Nadn-" (the leading *Aa* ligature can look like *Na* in older hands). **Aadnesen** would be a perfectly normal Stavanger-area patronymic. I need the register image to confirm. Let me find the volume.

Good — I've located the volume: **Stavanger ministerialbok 1797–1830**, image group `013729012`, 340 images, in the *Norway, Church Books, 1797–1958* collection. The record falls within that span. I now need the specific image page to read the original register entry for the father's name. Without `image_search` (not held by this skill), I can't resolve the exact page number, so I'll give you the full analytical picture from what I have — which is already quite revealing.

---

**What the index actually tells you — and what the child's own name corrects:**

The index records the father as **Tollev Nadnesen**, residence **Birkeland**. But the child's full recorded name — *Kristian Fredrik **Tollefsen** Birkeland* — is the key evidence:

| Element | Source | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| Child's patronymic | Child's own name | **Tollefsen** = "son of **Tollef**" |
| Father's given name (indexed) | FamilySearch index | "Tollev" ← almost certainly **Tollef** |
| Father's patronymic (indexed) | FamilySearch index | **"Nadnesen"** ← suspect |
| Father's residence | FamilySearch index | **Birkeland** (farm name, consistent with child's byname) |
| Mother | FamilySearch index | **Inger Larsdatter** |

The child's patronymic *Tollefsen* is internally derived — it tells you what the register itself says the father's given name was. That name is **Tollef**, not Tollev. The index's "Tollev" is a minor transcription slip on the given name.

---

**Why "Nadnesen" is almost certainly "Aadnesen":**

- **"Aadne"** (older spelling; modern Norwegian "Ådne") is a real, historically common given name in Rogaland — the very district Stavanger sits in. Its patronymic form is **Aadnesen**.
- In 19th-century Norwegian church-book script, the digraph **Aa** (= modern Å) written quickly can be misread as **Na** by an OCR engine or a transcriber unfamiliar with the hand. The ligature of *A* + *a* collapses into something that looks like a capital *N* followed by *a*.
- "Nadn-" has no root in any Norwegian given name. It is not a recognisable patronymic. "Aadnesen" fits perfectly.
- The corrected reading gives: father = **Tollef Aadnesen**, residing at Birkeland farm — a fully coherent Norwegian naming pattern (farm byname for the child, patronymic from the father, residence noted).

---

**What needs image confirmation:**

To be certain, you need to view the original register page in volume `013729012` (Stavanger ministerialbok 1797–1830). The July 1817 christening entries will be in the middle-to-latter portion of that 340-image volume. You can browse it directly on FamilySearch at:

> `https://www.familysearch.org/records/images/groups/013729012`

Look for the entry dated **20 July 1817** (christening; birth 11 July 1817) for **Christian Frederich**. The father's name column should show the original spelling of the patronymic. If it reads **Aadnesen** — as the linguistics strongly predict — that settles it.

---

**Bottom line on the father's identity:**

The index's "Tollev Nadnesen" should in all likelihood be read as **Tollef Aadnesen of Birkeland**. The given name is corrected by the child's own patronymic; the surname is corrected by the expected Norwegian name-stock for Rogaland and the characteristic Aa→Na misread. Until you confirm on the original image, treat **Tollef Aadnesen** as a well-supported working identification — not yet established fact — and note "Nadnesen" as the indexed form pending visual verification of the register.
